During bronchoconstriction (acute asthma attacks), the sensation of dyspnea (shortness of breath) arises from several factors:

2. Increased ventilatory drive 
3. Neural feedback from lung receptors

ICS work through their anti-inflammatory effects to prevent bronchoconstriction from occurring, but they do not acutely reverse bronchoconstriction once it has occurred. The perception of dyspnea during acute bronchoconstriction is more directly affected by bronchodilators (like beta-agonists) that can rapidly open airways.
